summary: The original hypotheses are plausible and well-grounded in stroke physiology and prior thrombolysis literature, but several need tighter interaction framing (explicitly stating which subgroup benefits more or less and why), clearer alignment with the SHAP directionality (which is weak here), more explicit conditionality (moderators: imaging core/penumbra, time-to-treatment, pre-stroke function, diabetes), and more concrete validation steps. I recommend revising all five feature hypotheses to sharpen treatment-response interaction claims, add measurable thresholds where supported by evidence, clarify uncertainties where SHAP mean values are near-zero or contradictory, and expand validation plans with feasible analyses within IST-3 or pooled data. Below are per-feature reviews and a fully revised FeatureHypothesesSet.

issues.message: Original 'bidirectional' framing is acceptable, but the mechanism reads as prognostic rather than an explicit treatment-response interaction. Must explicitly state which NIHSS bands derive greater absolute benefit from alteplase and why, and list moderators (time, imaging).
Validation suggestions are reasonable but should specify statistical models, interaction terms, and minimum sample/strata considerations.

per_mechanism.comments: Mechanism is biologically and clinically plausible: moderate severity often yields largest absolute benefit; very mild suffer ceiling effects; very severe may have large core and higher sICH. Must convert into a treatment-response interaction claim and include moderators (time-to-treatment, imaging core/penumbra).
per_mechanism.suggested_revision: Patients with moderate NIHSS (approx. 5-15) experience larger absolute benefit from IV alteplase than patients with very low (0-4) or very high (>20) NIHSS because they balance a substantial salvageable penumbra with lower baseline risk of symptomatic ICH; the magnitude of this interaction is conditional on short onset-to-treatment and imaging showing small core/large penumbra (i.e., among patients with small core on CT perfusion, even high NIHSS may still derive benefit). Validate using NIHSS×treatment interaction terms in logistic regression for mRS 0-2, adjusting for time-to-treatment and core volume, and estimate absolute risk differences within NIHSS bands.

per_feature.suggested_edits: Recast hypothesis as an explicit interaction: state which NIHSS bands benefit more/less, include numeric thresholds, and specify moderators and analytic approach.

issues.message: Original text notes moderators but should more explicitly present treatment-response claim and quantify age thresholds used (e.g., ≥80). Also align with SHAP which shows a small negative mean (older → less predicted benefit) but emphasize uncertainty.
Validation suggestions should include specific multivariable interaction model and recommended adjustment variables (pre-stroke mRS, imaging core, NIHSS, comorbidity index).

per_mechanism.comments: Mechanistic rationale (increased hemorrhage risk, frailty, competing mortality) is supported by IST-3 and pooled analyses. Must explicitly claim which elderly subgroups derive less absolute benefit (e.g., ≥80 with pre-stroke disability or large core) and which may still benefit (≥80 but independent pre-stroke, small core).
per_mechanism.suggested_revision: Older patients (commonly ≥80 years) tend to show smaller absolute net benefit from alteplase on average because higher baseline risk of sICH, frailty, and competing non-stroke mortality reduce the absolute improvement in independent survival; however, among elderly patients who are functionally independent pre-stroke and have small ischemic core / short onset-to-treatment, the relative efficacy may be preserved and yield clinically meaningful absolute benefit. Test age×treatment interaction (age continuous and categorical at ≥80) adjusting for pre-stroke mRS, NIHSS, imaging core, and time-to-treatment; report absolute risk differences and sICH contribution to net effect.

per_feature.suggested_edits: Quantify age thresholds and explicitly state conditionality by pre-stroke function and imaging; align with small negative SHAP mean but note uncertainty.

issues.message: SHAP mean for glucose is slightly positive (0.0023) while the hypothesis asserts hyperglycemia reduces benefit. Because SHAP magnitude is near-zero, this mismatch should be acknowledged and effect_direction set to 'unclear' or 'negative but uncertain'.
Biological mechanism is plausible, but need to distinguish acute stress hyperglycemia from chronic diabetes and to state thresholds for clinically meaningful effect (>10 mmol/L or >180 mg/dL).

per_mechanism.comments: Hyperglycemia is mechanistically linked to reperfusion injury and hemorrhagic transformation in preclinical and observational human studies, but trial-level evidence for effect modification is mixed. Must state this as a conditional interaction: higher admission glucose (e.g., >10 mmol/L) → smaller net benefit on average, especially in known diabetics or when glucose remains uncontrolled; but low SHAP amplitude indicates effect in this dataset is weak or inconsistent.
per_mechanism.suggested_revision: High admission glucose (practically >10 mmol/L / >180 mg/dL) likely attenuates the net benefit of alteplase because hyperglycemia increases reperfusion injury and blood–brain barrier breakdown, raising sICH risk and reducing functional gain; the effect is more pronounced in patients with chronic diabetes and when acute glucose is not rapidly corrected. Because SHAP signal here is small and slightly positive, treat glucose as an uncertain modifier and test glucose×treatment with adjustment for NIHSS, infarct size, and diabetes status; examine mediation by sICH and infarct growth.

per_feature.suggested_edits: Change effect_direction to 'unclear' (or 'negative but uncertain'), add numeric glucose thresholds, and emphasize distinguishing stress hyperglycemia vs chronic diabetes; propose mediation analyses and threshold/non-linear tests.

issues.message: Clinical interpretation is correct; main issue is treatment-response framing and conditional moderators (stroke location, imaging). Must explicitly define GCS cut-offs and how they interact with imaging and NIHSS.
Validation should suggest stratified analyses by anterior vs posterior circulation and use multivariable interaction models controlling for NIHSS and core volume.

per_mechanism.comments: Mechanism is plausible: low GCS often signals large infarct or brainstem compromise, lowering potential for functional recovery and possibly increasing hemorrhagic risk. But posterior strokes can have low GCS with salvageable tissue. Must state GCS thresholds (e.g., GCS ≤8) and conditionality by stroke subtype/imaging.
per_mechanism.suggested_revision: Patients with preserved consciousness (GCS 13-15) typically derive greater net benefit from alteplase compared with patients with deep impaired consciousness (GCS ≤8), because low GCS commonly indicates large established infarct or brain swelling that limits recoverable tissue and increases sICH/mortality risk. However, this interaction is moderated by stroke location — posterior circulation with low GCS may still show benefit if imaging demonstrates small core and treatable occlusion. Validate using GCS×treatment interaction models adjusted for NIHSS, stroke subtype (posterior vs anterior), and imaging core.

per_feature.suggested_edits: Make GCS a conditional modifier with numeric thresholds and explicit mention of location (posterior circulation exception); recommend stratified validation analyses.

issues.message: SHAP mean for weight is positive (0.0283), while hypothesis posits heavier patients may benefit less due to dose capping. The direction is unclear in the data; need to acknowledge SHAP signal and trial dosing policy (IST-3 dosing cap) before asserting direction.
Must specify whether IST-3 used a strict 90 mg cap and whether actual mg/kg dose records are available. Also consider body composition and confounding by comorbidity.

per_mechanism.comments: Mechanism (dose per kg effect and cap) is plausible; however the net effect direction depends on whether lower mg/kg reduces recanalization more than it reduces hemorrhage. Data from trials is mixed and may depend on whether dose capping was applied. Must frame as conditional and suggest direct analysis of mg/kg received and recanalization/sICH outcomes.
per_mechanism.suggested_revision: If a fixed maximum dose cap was applied (commonly 90 mg), very high-weight patients who received capped dosing may experience lower mg/kg exposure and therefore potentially less recanalization and smaller functional benefit on average; conversely, low-weight patients receive higher mg/kg exposure that could increase both efficacy and bleeding risk. Because the IST-3 SHAP signal is small and positive for weight, treat the direction as uncertain and test mg/kg×treatment and capped-dose×treatment interactions on recanalization, sICH, and functional outcome, adjusting for NIHSS and comorbidities.

per_feature.suggested_edits: Explicitly state the dependence on trial dosing cap and propose validating analyses using recorded dose/kg and cap status; change effect_direction to 'unclear' and emphasize confounding by obesity-related comorbidity.

revised.summary: Refined interaction hypotheses for top signals (NIHSS, age, glucose, GCS, weight) focus on treatment-response differences: specify which subgroups derive greater or smaller absolute benefit from IV alteplase and why (biological mechanism), list key moderators (time-to-treatment, imaging core/penumbra, pre-stroke function, diabetes, dose cap), and provide concrete validation plans. Note that SHAP mean effects are small in this dataset (near-zero), so these remain mechanistic hypotheses to be tested rather than confirmed effect modifiers.

feature_hypotheses.clinical_interpretation: Baseline NIH Stroke Scale quantifying neurological deficit (stroke severity).
feature_hypotheses.why_important: Severity determines salvageable tissue vs established infarct and predicts sICH risk; these change the absolute net benefit of reperfusion therapy.

mechanisms.description: Treatment-response interaction claim: Patients with moderate baseline NIHSS (approx. 515) gain the largest absolute benefit from IV alteplase because they are most likely to have sizable salvageable penumbra with lower sICH risk; patients with very low NIHSS (0) gain little absolute benefit due to high baseline independence (ceiling effect); patients with very high NIHSS (>20) generally derive less net benefit because large established core and higher sICH/mortality reduce functional gains. Crucially, this NIHSS×treatment effect is conditional on time-to-treatment and imaging: among patients with small core/large penumbra on CT perfusion or MRI, even high-NIHSS patients may still derive substantial benefit.

feature_hypotheses.subgroup_implications: Prioritize treatment for moderate NIHSS (515) within short onset-to-treatment windows and with favorable imaging; expect limited absolute benefit in very mild or very severe NIHSS unless imaging shows small core.
validation_suggestions: Fit logistic regression for mRS 0-2 at 6 months with NIHSS×treatment interaction (NIHSS continuous and categorical bands 0-4, 5-15, 16-20, >20), adjusting for age, time-to-treatment, imaging core volume, and pre-stroke mRS.
Report absolute risk differences and NNT within NIHSS bands; test heterogeneity via likelihood-ratio test of interaction term.
Perform sensitivity analyses restricting to patients with CT perfusion/MRI to evaluate NIHSS×core-volume×treatment three-way interaction.
caveats: NIHSS is influenced by infarct location (posterior strokes can have low NIHSS but large penumbra) which can confound simple NIHSS stratification.
Small SHAP mean (near zero) implies limited signal in this model; interaction tests may be underpowered without pooled data.
Residual confounding by unmeasured imaging or comorbidity features is possible even in randomized sample if interactions with treatment are complex.

feature_hypotheses.why_important: Age-related vascular fragility, comorbidity, frailty, and competing mortality alter the absolute benefit-to-harm trade-off for thrombolysis.

mechanisms.description: Treatment-response interaction claim: Older patients (commonly defined ≥80 years) tend to have smaller absolute net benefit from IV alteplase on average because higher sICH risk, frailty, and non-stroke competing mortality reduce gains from reperfusion; however, among elderly patients who are functionally independent pre-stroke (pre-stroke mRS 0-1) and who have small ischemic core and short onset-to-treatment, relative efficacy is often preserved and can translate into meaningful absolute benefit. Thus the age×treatment interaction is moderated by pre-stroke function, imaging core size, and time-to-treatment.

feature_hypotheses.subgroup_implications: Expect attenuated absolute benefit and higher harm in very elderly with pre-existing disability or large core; do not reflexively withhold alteplase from all older patients—those with good pre-stroke function and favorable imaging may still benefit.
validation_suggestions: Estimate age×treatment interaction with age as continuous and categorical (e.g., <65, 65�79, ≥80), adjusting for pre-stroke mRS, NIHSS, imaging core, and time-to-treatment.
Report absolute risk differences and sICH-attributable harm by age strata; consider subgroup analyses restricted to independent pre-stroke patients.
If sample size limited, pool IST-3 with other trials (individual patient data meta-analysis) to improve power for age-stratified interaction testing.
caveats: Age correlates with multiple mediators (comorbidity, vessel fragility); observed interactions may reflect these factors rather than age per se.
IST-3 and pooled analyses show mixed results; age alone is insufficient to determine treatment eligibility.

feature_hypotheses.why_important: Hyperglycemia promotes reperfusion injury, blood-brain barrier breakdown, and infarct growth, potentially increasing sICH risk and reducing functional gains after thrombolysis.

mechanisms.description: Treatment-response interaction claim (conditional and uncertain): Patients with marked hyperglycemia on admission (e.g., >10 mmol/L / >180 mg/dL) — particularly those with known diabetes or persistent hyperglycemia in-hospital — are likely to have attenuated net benefit from alteplase because hyperglycemia amplifies reperfusion injury and hemorrhagic transformation; conversely, normoglycemic patients are more likely to translate reperfusion into functional recovery. This interaction is moderated by diabetes status, infarct size, and whether acute glucose is rapidly corrected.

feature_hypotheses.subgroup_implications: Expect smaller absolute benefit and potentially higher sICH in patients with admission glucose >10 mmol/L and in poorly controlled diabetics; normoglycemic patients likely realize greater net functional improvement per unit reperfusion, though the dataset's SHAP signal is small/uncertain.
validation_suggestions: Test glucose×treatment interaction with glucose modeled continuously and with thresholds (e.g., ≤7, 7-10, >10 mmol/L), adjusting for NIHSS, diabetes status, imaging core size, and time-to-treatment.
Perform mediation analyses to determine how much of any interaction is explained by sICH and infarct growth (assess CT/MRI volumetrics if available).
If available, analyze whether in-hospital glucose control (insulin protocols) modifies the interaction.
caveats: Acute stress hyperglycemia can be a marker of stroke severity and physiological stress; without careful adjustment for NIHSS and infarct size the interaction may be confounded.
SHAP mean in this dataset is small and slightly positive, indicating weak or inconsistent signal—treat this hypothesis as exploratory.

feature_hypotheses.clinical_interpretation: Glasgow Coma Scale score at baseline (level of consciousness).
feature_hypotheses.why_important: Level of consciousness reflects extent and location of brain injury; it conditions the amount of salvageable tissue and the risk of hemorrhagic conversion and death after thrombolysis.

mechanisms.description: Treatment-response interaction claim: Patients with preserved consciousness (GCS 1315) are more likely to obtain net benefit from IV alteplase because preserved GCS typically indicates smaller core and higher chance of functional recovery; patients with deep reduced consciousness (GCS ≤8) generally derive less benefit or may be harmed due to large established infarct, mass effect, or high sICH risk. The interaction is moderated by stroke location — posterior circulation strokes may present with low GCS yet still have salvageable tissue and hence may not follow this pattern.

feature_hypotheses.subgroup_implications: Predict larger net benefit in patients with GCS 1315 and early treatment; expect attenuated benefit or higher harm among GCS ≤8 unless imaging shows small core (especially in posterior circulation).
validation_suggestions: Model GCS×treatment interaction (GCS continuous and dichotomized at ≤8 vs >8, and alternative bands) adjusting for NIHSS, stroke subtype (posterior vs anterior), and imaging core volume.
Compare sICH, mortality, and functional outcome across GCS strata in randomized arms and perform sensitivity analyses excluding non-ischemic causes of reduced consciousness.
If sample sizes allow, test three-way interactions GCS×stroke-location×treatment.
caveats: Low GCS may be caused by stroke mimics (seizure, hypoglycemia) and by sedation—misclassification can bias results.
GCS correlates with NIHSS and infarct location; observed modification may be mediated or confounded by these factors.

feature_hypotheses.clinical_interpretation: Patient body weight used to calculate alteplase dose (typically 0.9 mg/kg) and subject to maximum dosing caps.
feature_hypotheses.why_important: Weight determines mg/kg exposure; if a fixed maximum dose is applied, high-weight patients receive lower mg/kg which may reduce recanalization and net efficacy, while low-weight patients receive higher mg/kg and may have increased bleeding risk.

mechanisms.description: Treatment-response interaction claim (conditional): If IST-3 applied a fixed maximum alteplase dose (e.g., 90 mg), very high-weight patients who were dose-capped may have lower mg/kg exposure and therefore reduced recanalization probability and smaller net functional benefit; low-weight patients may receive higher mg/kg and thus higher efficacy but also greater hemorrhagic risk. The net effect direction depends on whether reduced mg/kg leads to clinically meaningful reductions in recanalization that outweigh any reduction in bleeding.

feature_hypotheses.subgroup_implications: Anticipate potential attenuation of benefit in very high-weight/capped patients and a shifted benefit-harm balance in low-weight patients; effect will depend on actual dosing practice and body composition.
validation_suggestions: Use recorded alteplase dose to compute mg/kg and analyze mg/kg×treatment interaction on recanalization (if angiographic data), sICH, and 6-month independence, adjusting for NIHSS, age, and comorbidities.
Stratify by whether actual dose was capped; perform comparison of outcomes in capped vs non-capped patients within weight strata.
If available, examine pharmacodynamic proxies (recanalization rates, early neurological improvement) rather than only final mRS.
caveats: Weight may proxy for obesity-related comorbidity (diabetes, hypertension) which could confound interactions.
IST-3 dosing policy must be checked: if no strict cap was applied or cap was rare, hypothesized effect may be irrelevant to this cohort.
SHAP mean is small and positive in this dataset, so observed association may be weak or reflect correlated factors.

revised.cross_feature_patterns: Key conditional interactions to test: NIHSS×age (very severe stroke in very elderly likely produces especially attenuated net benefit), NIHSS/GCS×imaging core (severity/consciousness modify benefit mainly when core is large), glucose×diabetes status (stress hyperglycemia vs chronic hyperglycemia differ), and weight×dose-cap (weight effect depends on whether a dose cap was applied). Prioritize multivariable interaction models and mediation analyses (sICH, recanalization, infarct growth) and consider pooling IST-3 with other trials for power.
